item.description: Fuente: NASA.

item.title: NASA systems engineering team details Habitable Worlds Observatory mission architecture
item.description: Finding an Earth-like world beyond the solar system is the holy grail of exoplanet research, and the field has seen remarkable technological advances in detecting and studying exoplanets since the first confirmed exoplanet around a sun-like star was discovered in 1995. These advances include ground- and space-based telescopes, notably the James Webb Space Telescope. Although astronomers have already directly imaged some exoplanets, directly imaging Earth-like planets around sun-like stars remains a major technological challenge, primarily because these planets are extremely faint compared… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 2024 solar storm triggered ultrarelativistic electrons inside Earth's 'impenetrable barrier'
item.description: The Earth is surrounded by an invisible barrier that was thought to prevent highly energetic electrons from reaching closer to our planet. But in 2024, Japan's Arase space probe detected these electrons well inside the barrier. Now, research led by Nagoya University has found evidence that the electrons were accelerated locally rather than infiltrating from outer radiation belts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Webb Sees Turbulent Star Nursery
item.description: In this Webb image released on Oct. 22, 2026, we see a turbulent cauldron of star formation filled with dense clumps of gas. This region is named N159 and is located 161,000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the satellite galaxies orbiting the Milky Way galaxy. This region has a lower metallicity […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Refugees' experiences of loss shape their business ambitions
item.description: The severity of the losses refugees experience can shape the kinds of businesses they build in a new country, according to a qualitative study by Tilburg University researcher Kurian George and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Portable device accurately and rapidly detects PFAS in water
item.description: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are synthetic chemicals known for their exceptional resistance to degradation, earning them the nickname "forever chemicals." These persistent substances can accumulate in water, soil and living organisms, raising concerns about their potential impacts on human health and the environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can gravitational fields break and reconnect? Einstein's equations suggest they can
item.description: More than a century after Einstein first devised the equations that describe gravity, physicists are still finding new ways of interpreting them. Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, recently found a new way of looking at Einstein's equations that reveals a striking analogy with "magnetic reconnection" in plasmas, which occurs when magnetic field lines break and reconnect, powering explosive phenomena such as solar flares. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Europa: el calor del verano de 2026 dejó más de 50.000 muertos
item.description: Más de 50.000 personas murieron por causas relacionadas con el calor en las ciudades europeas durante el verano de 2026, según una nueva investigación científica. El estudio estima que alrededor de dos tercios de esos fallecimientos son atribuibles al calentamiento provocado por la actividad humana. Italia, Francia y España registraron las cifras más elevadas de mortalidad. Los investigadores advierten de que el balance podría ser aún mayor: el análisis abarca 854 áreas urbanas de 30 países, que representan aproximadamente el 40% de su población. ¿Qué revela este verano sobre el impacto del… Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: María Clara Calle Aguirre

item.title: Launch of global seed platform to tackle native seed bottleneck holding back nature restoration
item.description: On Oct. 13, the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (RBG Kew) launched the Seed Portal for Online Data (SeedPOD), a new open-access platform designed to tackle bottlenecks affecting global ecological restoration, by making native seed collections and the knowledge needed to grow them easier to discover. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Japan's genome-editing law sets a global ethics challenge
item.description: A Hiroshima University researcher contends that Japan's newly enacted law regulating human genome-edited embryos and germ cells marks a significant advance in the governance of reproductive genome editing. Tsutomu Sawai, professor at Hiroshima University's Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, praises the new law for defining prohibited activities and penalties for violation but also stresses the need for stronger international coordination to prevent the prohibitions from being circumvented by individuals seeking procedures abroad. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Against all expectations, researchers control the magnetic core of a single atom
item.description: Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have succeeded in controlling the magnetism in the nucleus of a single atom with radio waves. This came as a surprise: until now, physicists believed that this nuclear spin could not be manipulated directly. The discovery could open up new possibilities for storing and reading quantum information. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nature-inspired additive could help protect living cells during freezing and thawing
item.description: In Australia, around 2,000 people are on the waiting list to receive an organ transplant, but thanks to new research being undertaken at the University of New England (UNE), this number could someday be significantly reduced. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
item.description: When a star like our sun grows old, it puffs up into a red giant that can gobble up its nearest planets. But Chinese astronomers say they have found three solar systems where planets should have been eaten this way yet somehow survived – a puzzle that could change how scientists picture Earth’s distant future. Using Nasa’s TESS space telescope, a team led by Qian Shengbang from Yunnan University showed that three Jupiter-like planets – each hugging an ageing star in the northern sky – had lived... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: A 60-year search is over: Chemists isolate long-elusive molecules with boron-oxygen triple bonds
item.description: In a new publication in the journal Nature Chemistry, chemists in professor Holger Braunschweig's team at the University of Würzburg, supported by computational work from the team of professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University in India, detail their discovery of a method for preparing and isolating a range of surprisingly stable oxoboranes—a challenge that has stood for over 60 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky—this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
item.description: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects? It's earwax. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Amber fossils reveal how ancient Australian landmass helped seed Southeast Asia's tropical forests
item.description: A landmass that broke away from northwestern Australia about 150 million years ago and drifted north for the next 100 million years helped lay the foundations for Southeast Asia's extraordinarily diverse tropical forests, new research has revealed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Minnesota farmer finds 11-foot metal object suspected to be Chinese rocket debris
item.description: Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Indonesia's El Niño–driven peat fires are choking the region—and releasing centuries of stored carbon
item.description: Right now, people in parts of Indonesia are inhaling what may be the most polluted atmosphere on Earth. As the historically large 2026 El Niño intensifies, parts of Southeast Asia have been plunged into an air quality crisis of catastrophic proportions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Do spiders dream? Researchers studying spiders have found sleep patterns resembling REM sleep
item.description: A recent study on Australian jumping spiders has uncovered that these creatures undergo unique sleep stages, reminiscent of REM sleep. The observed sleep patterns, characterized by distinct periods of stillness interspersed with muscle movements and eye twitches, suggest that spiders possess more advanced sleep mechanisms than previously believed. Future research aims to explore their natural sleeping behaviors, offering insights into the links between sleep and cognitive processes across species. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: National parenting support strategy could strengthen Australia's efforts to protect children
item.description: Australia has no shortage of policies relating to children. In fact, these policies are often in the headlines. Billions of dollars are invested each year trying to improve outcomes for children and young people. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Parts of Tibetan Plateau's frozen ground are gaining ice despite warming
item.description: High on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, the ground stays frozen, with only the top few meters melting each summer. Although the region is warming about twice as fast as the global average, a new study finds that more than a third of its permafrost, mainly in the central plateau, has gained ice since 2000. Stronger westerly winds bring more rain and snow, which seeps into the ground in summer and freezes again in winter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a hidden defense mechanism in aging muscles that sacrifices strength to protect cells from damage. In mice, partially restoring a crucial molecule reversed signs of muscle wasting and prevented premature death, raising hopes for new treatments for age-related muscle decline. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: When consumers search 'cyclospora,' bagged salad sales take the hit
item.description: This year, the U.S. saw its highest annual count of confirmed Cyclospora cases, roughly 20,000, according to the CDC. New research published in Risk Analysis examines outbreaks from 2018 to 2022 and finds that the retail losses associated with these events vary with how much public attention the outbreak draws. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ants prioritize brain energy during starvation, echoing pattern seen in humans
item.description: The human brain accounts for roughly 2% of total body weight but uses approximately 20% of our body's energy. Relative to our body size, human brains are much larger than those of other mammals and take a lot of energy to keep humans going. The evolution of our unusually large "social brain" is thought to have given us advanced intelligence and enabled the formation of large, complex societies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New feed supplement addresses honey bee declines after blueberry pollination
item.description: Washington produces more blueberries than any other U.S. state, but farmers sometimes struggle to obtain honey bees to pollinate the plants and produce fruit. That's in part because beekeepers are reluctant to provide bees to blueberry farms, given that there have been increased—and mysterious—bee colony losses after blueberry pollination. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Smaller EV batteries, longer range? Scientists may have found a way
item.description: Scientists have developed a new technology that could make electric vehicle batteries smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting, potentially allowing cars to travel farther on a single charge. By borrowing precision manufacturing techniques from computer chip production, they found a way to prevent damaging lithium buildup that has held back next-generation batteries. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a secret glow in toxic fire salamanders
item.description: Researchers have discovered a surprising hidden ability in Europe's familiar black-and-yellow fire salamanders: they glow green and cyan under ultraviolet light. The mysterious fluorescence comes mainly from glands in their skin and their toxic secretions, which can continue glowing for more than 24 hours after being released. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a long-lost volcanic system in Iran that dates back roughly 100 million years, revealing a hidden chapter in Earth's tectonic history. The discovery sheds new light on the disappearance of an ancient ocean and the powerful geological forces that reshaped the Middle East. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Sound-levitated particles reveal how static charge builds up
item.description: When two objects touch and then separate, they can swap tiny amounts of electric charge, even if they are made from exactly the same material. This 'triboelectric effect' is the source of everyday static electricity, but it is still poorly understood in large samples of powder, where vast numbers of particles are constantly colliding with each other. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds heat waves speed snowmelt substantially, but rivers respond unevenly
item.description: A new study by researchers at Montana State University has found that heat waves substantially accelerate the melting rate of mountain snowpack; however, the resulting water doesn't necessarily produce an immediate increase in streamflow. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unos científicos desarrollan un dispositivo capaz de unir la luz de varios telescopios y lo probarán en Calar Alto, Almería
item.description: La astronomía ha evolucionado muchísimo en los últimos años. Cada vez se pueden captar objetos más difusos y lejanos , pero todo tiene un límite. Para llegar más lejos, es necesario que los telescopios puedan captar más luz. Eso se consigue con telescopios más grandes, pero, técnicamente hablando, es algo que tiene un límite. Por eso, la ciencia se centra también en la búsqueda de formas de combinar la luz de muchos telescopios pequeños en una sola señal que los instrumentos puedan manipular. Justamente eso es lo que pretende hacer un equipo internacional de científicos, dirigido por el… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Fishmeal alternative aims to protect marine wildlife from overfishing
item.description: Technology that transforms organic waste into animal feed could help ease an overreliance on fishmeal in aquaculture. University of Queensland researchers have developed a production process that converts organic waste into biogas to grow a high-protein alternative to fish feed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Luxury round-the-world cruise ends abruptly as fuel costs skyrocket
item.description: Cruise operator Villa Vie Residences said it would disembark passengers and crew, and restructure its business due to soaring fuel costs. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: Dead tree branches rise and fall with changing humidity, laser scans reveal
item.description: Dead tree branches are by no means static but move throughout the day. Geoinformatics researchers at Heidelberg University tracked these movements in a study conducted in cooperation with the Finnish Geospatial Research Institute (FGI). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between Earth's opposite poles that may help explain how the planet plunged into past ice ages. New research suggests that as massive ice sheets expanded across the Northern Hemisphere, they cooled Atlantic Ocean waters that eventually traveled south toward Antarctica. This cooling may have disrupted Southern Ocean circulation, allowing the ocean to absorb and store more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, further cooling the planet. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Machine learning simulations reveal how plastic transforms into hard carbon
item.description: In a new study published in Chemical Science, researchers from the University of Oxford's Department of Chemistry have used machine learning simulations to trace how a common polymer transforms into hard carbon, revealing the atomic-scale processes that give this technologically important material its disordered structure. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why do people self-harm? The mind-body divide might hold some clues
item.description: In Finnish lore, the goddess Kivutar stashes away pain in a mountain for safekeeping. And yet she's also a healer, channeling it into rocks or boiling it down into a less potent form in a huge vat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon
item.description: NASA’s Artemis I mission has revealed that cosmic radiation near the Moon is higher than in Earth orbit, but not by as much as scientists might expect. Tiny experimental detectors also uncovered surprising details about how radiation passes through the human body, offering valuable insights for future lunar exploration. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: U.S. moves to weaken methane limits on oil and gas producers
item.description: U.S. President Donald Trump announced Tuesday a sweeping rollback of rules that stop oil and gas producers from emitting methane, a greenhouse gas superpollutant. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cyclone eases after lashing India coast, no deaths reported
item.description: Ferocious winds and torrential rain lashed India's southeastern coast after a cyclone made landfall on Wednesday, but officials said there were no initial reports of deaths and the storm later began to ease. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Comets probably didn't seed life on Earth after all, new study suggests
item.description: The theory that comets delivered the molecular building blocks for life on Earth is a long-standing one, since comets are known to carry many of these molecules. However, a new study challenges this idea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Antarctica’s “Doomsday Glacier” could raise sea levels twice as much as predicted
item.description: Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier may be melting twice as much as previously predicted, even without additional global warming. Scientists discovered that warm ocean water is penetrating miles beneath the ice, weakening its foundations and accelerating its retreat. A new model predicts that the glacier could add up to 30 millimeters to global sea levels by 2100, with a 60% chance of losing a crucial stabilizing ridge. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: EEUU acaba de revelar que China tiene un avión secreto orbitando en el espacio desde seis hace años
item.description: Durante años, una fotografía tomada en el espacio alimentó las sospechas de que China había conseguido desarrollar su propia versión de uno de los vehículos militares más secretos de Estados Unidos. La imagen circulaba por internet, había aparecido incluso en una presentación de la Fuerza Espacial estadounidense y nadie había confirmado públicamente qué mostraba exactamente. Ahora, un informe de la inteligencia militar de Washington ha resuelto el misterio: Pekín dispone de un avión espacial reutilizable extraordinariamente parecido al X-37B estadounidense . Y los detalles que han salido a la… Fuente: Xataka.

item.description: Professional analysts chose options that matched AI assistant's preference 86 percent of the time, research finds. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.

item.title: After 1,600 years, researchers recreate the colour-changing glass of a Roman masterpiece
item.description: A team of researchers has made a groundbreaking achievement by replicating the color-shifting glass of the ancient Roman Lycurgus Cup. Created 1,600 years ago, this unique glass displays stunning optical effects thanks to its tiny gold and silver nanoparticles. Their rigorous experimentation with both ancient and modern techniques opens doors for scientific advancements, extending beyond mere artistic creation. A modern sculpture inspired by this historic artifact will soon be unveiled. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks
item.description: A national monument since the 1920s, Chiricahua is America’s newest national park. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength
item.description: A new clinical trial suggests that a simple daily fiber supplement could significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis pain, improve muscle strength, and make the body less sensitive to pain. Researchers discovered that the benefits may be linked to changes in gut bacteria and the hormone GLP-1, revealing a promising new approach to arthritis relief. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: MapInsights helps police trainees learn the territory
item.description: In early 2026, the University of Illinois Division of Public Safety was facing a challenge. It had 11 security guards it planned to convert to community service officers, which meant they would change from being based in one building to working a whole beat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
item.description: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Digital tools and 3D printing emerge as key themes in circular economy research
item.description: A review of the research literature spanning the years 2020 to 2026 has found that digital technologies, additive manufacturing and resource recovery are major themes in the transition toward a sustainable, circular economy. The work, published in the International Journal of Services and Operations Management, highlights the need for more cooperation between businesses and other stakeholders and for better governmental policies to ease the transition. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Halloween meets history in many ghostly tourism attractions. Is this a problem?
item.description: Halloween, the fall holiday and $13.5 billion industry, lurks around the corner. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Brambles are a problem weed in South Africa, but researchers are closer to finding a natural enemy to manage them
item.description: Invasive alien brambles have been spreading across South Africa since the early 1900s, having come from North America and Europe. All brambles fall within the genus Rubus. Their common names in South Africa are braam (Afrikaans), ijingijolo (isiZulu) and monoko-metsi (seSotho). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world
item.description: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have set the stage for ants to conquer the planet, with a surprising boost from “jumping genes” hidden in their DNA. Scientists discovered that bursts of activity from these mobile genetic elements coincided with the rise of major ant groups and may have helped sharpen their extraordinary ability to communicate through smell. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Researchers produce urea in the field using system powered by biobatteries and solar energy
item.description: The CONFETI project, coordinated by the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona (UAB), has concluded three years of research with the commissioning of a pilot system capable of producing urea, a nitrogen fertilizer widely used in agriculture, directly in the field using renewable energy. This fertilizer is produced from carbon dioxide (CO₂) and nitrates in an electrochemical reactor powered by energy from biobatteries and solar panels. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Researchers discover why some frogs have escaped the current amphibian mass extinction
item.description: Amphibians are the most threatened vertebrates on Earth, with 41% of species facing extinction. In the highlands of Central and South America, a killer fungus has wiped out much of the once-abundant amphibian diversity. Yet in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, an isolated mountain range in northern Colombia, amphibians still thrive. The mountain range is home to a remarkable amphibian community of at least 48 species, including 25 found nowhere else on the planet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Injuries matter less in the NFL than you think
item.description: New research from Northwestern's Kellogg School of Management finds that injury matters less in the NFL than is often assumed. With the exception of highly paid quarterbacks, losing players—even the high-dollar ones—to injury is not as fatal to a team's success as one might think. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover the immune system’s hidden sense of touch
item.description: Scientists at McGill University have discovered a surprising new ability of immune cells that could change how we understand long-term immunity. Researchers found that T cells can actually sense how stiff their surrounding tissues are, using these physical signals to help determine whether they develop into long-lasting memory cells that protect against future infections. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Cost overruns aren't just due to incompetence, bureaucracy and bad faith
item.description: Nine out of 10 major transportation projects go over their initial budget. This isn't always because of incompetence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Punishment alone won't help gang‑involved teens—a former child soldier explains why
item.description: When Americans hear of child soldiers, they may imagine tragic images of children wielding rifles on distant battlefields. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02202-3 A jury weighs in on whether teaching assessments are popularity contests or an important tool. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: We studied 1,584 data centers—and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth
item.description: Data centers require enormous investments: land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure. Yet, once they're up and running, they tend to employ no more than a few dozen people in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are asking what they will get in return. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossil fuel ad ban could 'jeopardise' TDU village, SA government says
item.description: A ban on oil, coal and gas company ads from public spaces in Adelaide CBD including bus stops, banners and billboards is approved by the city council, with the instigator of the motion saying local government has an obligation to tackle "fossil fuel sponsorship". Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Sharne Wakefield

item.title: The way Earth's 'thermostat' works may have changed during Pangea era
item.description: Life arose on Earth at least 3.5 billion years ago, and our planet has remained habitable ever since—not too hot, not too cold. These life-sustaining conditions are possible in part thanks to a built-in, carbon cycle–based climate "thermostat" that controls the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: EEUU deja en vilo la tregua comercial con la UE por los fondos a Airbus
item.description: Washington alega que el préstamo récord del BEI a la firma aeroespacial comunitaria le da ventaja frente a Boeing Leer Fuente: Expansión - Economía.

item.title: Identical vesicles, different behaviors: Model reveals how spontaneous asymmetry gives rise to lifelike behavior
item.description: In nonreciprocal active matter, agents act differently on each other, seemingly in violation of Newton's third law. This principle can result in various active matter traits, such as self-propulsion, molecular regulation and collective motion. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can your brain make you see ghosts? The science behind the Bloody Mary legend
item.description: It's Halloween night. Someone has dared you to turn off the lights and stand in front of the mirror. The rules are simple: Stare into your reflection and say her name three times. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 'simple recipe' takes some of the guesswork out of mass spectrometry imaging
item.description: A small sample of human tissue can hold a remarkable amount of information. Researchers can use it to search for molecular clues associated with cancer, investigate the chemical landscape of the brain or determine where a drug travels after it enters the body. Mass spectrometry imaging, or MSI, helps answer those questions by mapping where different molecules are located within tissue. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rubin Observatory reveals its first dwarf planet candidate in our solar system
item.description: Scientists may add a new dwarf planet to the official roster of our solar system. The distant, icy body, provisionally dubbed 2026 ED138, orbits our system beyond Pluto. It was spotted earlier this month by a scientist combing through data from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3 out of 4 responses to UK smoke-free generation consultation were AI bot-generated
item.description: Three-quarters of all the responses to the U.K.'s public consultation in 2023 on creating a smoke-free generation and restricting disposable vape sales were generated by AI bots, finds an analysis of publicly available data and freedom of information requests, published online in the journal Tobacco Control. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Open database tracks Earth's water cycle by standardizing decades of satellite data
item.description: All water comes from somewhere. Researchers who want to know where it comes from rely on water isotopes, variants of water molecules with slightly different masses, as location identifiers. In particular, the specific ratio of heavy to light water isotopes is unique to the water's origin and processes it has undergone and can provide information on how water travels across the globe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can planting trees on riverbanks save salmon rivers from global warming?
item.description: Every summer, Québec rivers increasingly reach water temperature levels that threaten Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). Just a few extra degrees can make the difference between a favorable and hostile habitat for this iconic species. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Counteranion captures reactants to boost light-driven chemistry in dilute solutions
item.description: Researchers at Kyushu University have developed a photocatalytic system that can selectively capture reacting molecules and hold them close to the active sites that absorb energy from light. This innovation addresses a long-standing challenge of having the photocatalyst maintain a high reaction rate even when the reacting molecules are present at very low concentrations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Double debris disk orbiting a dead star hints at our solar system's future
item.description: Astronomers using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT) have found a rare disk of debris around a dead star that provides a glimpse of what may happen to our solar system. Unlike in similar systems previously found, the debris—the leftovers of planets that once orbited the star—is organized in a double disk, the two parts separated by a clear gap. The disk appears to be shaped by two planetary bodies, one possibly as big as Pluto, that have survived the violent death of the star. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bottom trawlers do huge damage to life on undersea mountains. Could an end finally be in sight?
item.description: Tens of thousands of underwater mountains dot the ocean floor around the world. A few break the surface, such as the Hawaiian island chain. The rest are seamounts, peaks and pinnacles rising from the deep seafloor. Some lie just a few meters below the surface, while others rest deeper. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New cacao variety could help protect global chocolate supply from disease
item.description: Chocolate lovers may not realize it, but the future of one of the world's most popular foods is increasingly under pressure. Diseases, shifting weather patterns and other environmental stressors are threatening cacao production globally, contributing to supply concerns and economic challenges for the millions of farmers who grow the crop that makes chocolate possible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Supporting children with dyslexia starts with preparing their teachers
item.description: A child pauses at a word, tries it, then looks to the teacher for help. Telling the word to the child can get the sentence moving. Working out what to teach so the child can read similar words independently takes a different kind of expertise. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI and satellite data could give Florida earlier warnings of toxic red tides
item.description: Red tide, a harmful algal bloom that produces toxins, is known for causing respiratory irritation in humans and killing fish in coastal waters. Recent research shows that the conversation is also shifting to include a more subtle neurological threat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists uncover new way to control magnetism and topology using light in atomically thin materials
item.description: Envision a material whose magnetic properties and electronic topology can be toggled by exposure to light, paving the way for future electronic devices that do not rely on traditional electrical switching, which wastes energy by producing heat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Extreme risk protection orders are designed to prevent gun violence. But how do they impact the people subject to them?
item.description: About 125 people die from gun violence through homicide or suicide in the United States every day. Many more are injured by firearms. Extreme risk protection orders (ERPOs), known in California as gun violence restraining orders, are designed to keep firearms temporarily away from people at risk of harming themselves or others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Potential antimalarial compound discovered in institute's microbe collection
item.description: Scientists hunting for a new malaria treatment may have found a solution within a historical natural compound collection housed at The Herbert Wertheim UF Scripps Institute for Biomedical Innovation & Technology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Kimmy Kim ha comentado: Yes not for Halloween BUT for Hollywood indeed
item.description: Are you stepping into a spacesuit this week? We are — but not for Halloween! Tune in on Thursday, Oct. 29, to watch NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA... Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Electricity is rising because we’re phasing￼ out fossil fuels and implementing green energy, which is much more expensive, especially in the northeast sector of the United States…
item.description: Electricity is rising because we’re phasing￼ out fossil fuels and implementing green energy, which is much more expensive, especially in the northeast sector of the United States. ￼ Barry Ridgeway Fuente: CBS News.

item.title: Light-controlled brake makes random molecular motion 300,000 times slower
item.description: Molecules are never still. Driven by thermal energy, they are constantly moving through space, while their individual parts also rotate relative to one another. Scientists at IOCB Prague have now shown that random motion within a molecule can be dramatically suppressed. Using light, they can slow down the relative rotation of two different parts of a single molecule by up to five orders of magnitude, paving the way for more complex molecular machines. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: People are influenced by unreliable information yet remain aware of its influence on their decisions
item.description: Every day, people make decisions based on information obtained from social media, news outlets, online reviews and interpersonal communication, all of which vary in reliability. Numerical indicators and labels designed to convey information reliability, such as user ratings and fact-checking systems, have become increasingly common online. However, an important question remains: When reliability is explicitly stated, do people use this information appropriately for making decisions? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Museum visits are generally not perceived as boring, study finds
item.description: Museums are regarded as places of inspiration and cultural experience—boredom is not the first thing that springs to mind. However, an international team of researchers led by Thomas Götz from the University of Vienna has now, for the first time, systematically investigated how frequently boredom occurs during museum visits. The team found that while visitors are, on average, only slightly bored, this boredom has a negative impact on knowledge acquisition and their assessment of the museum visit. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A brief-ish history of METI. Part I: Early ideas and experiments
item.description: Long before modern astronomy, humans looked to the stars and were astounded by what they saw. Even by the most ancient reckoning, the night sky offered enough to inspire awe and wonder, make us feel insignificant, fire our imaginations and foster hope and a sense of connection. Yet, for as long as humans have surveyed the heavens, they have seen no indication that life as we know it exists elsewhere—what has come to be known as the "Great Silence." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny droplets use pressure to unlock new routes to degradable plastics
item.description: Using a new technique, a research group led by Osaka Metropolitan University (OMU) has substantially increased the range of plastics that can be degraded naturally. The study is published in the journal Macromolecules. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Energy prices are rising — and the impact goes far beyond the gas pump. CBS News' Kelly O'Grady breaks down how global conflicts, higher diesel costs and rising electri... Ver más

Ver más Electricity is rising because we’re phasing￼ out fossil fuels and implementing green energy, which is much more expensive, especially in the northeast sector of the United States. ￼ Tenemos problemas para reproducir… Fuente: CBS News.

item.title: The beacon effect: Rethinking what it means to make an impression
item.description: When people think about making a good impression at work, the focus usually turns inward. How do I present myself? How do I demonstrate my value? How do I make sure others see me as capable, confident and influential? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new survey of Canadian English shows what has changed in 50 years
item.description: Over the past 50 years, Canadian English has become more uniform across regions and has adopted many American terms and pronunciations, while the use of Canadian spellings has gained in popularity. These are the key results of a large-scale study by McGill researchers to update the Survey of Canadian English, initially done in 1972. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How we rewrite memories of fallen artists—but not their art
item.description: What happens to our memories when we learn disturbing news about a beloved artist? New research from the University of South Florida finds that after a scandal, the brain tricks us: it reconciles a fallen artist with their adored art by rewriting our memories in two completely different directions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Urban infrastructure grows more slowly than population, global analysis finds
item.description: As cities grow in population, they grow proportionally in terms of infrastructure—new buildings, paved streets and parking lots. Or so says conventional wisdom. However, a new study by a team of New York University researchers dispels this thinking. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Antarctic rocks reveal a missing chapter of glacier history
item.description: Antarctica's glaciers were changing long before satellites, weather stations or cameras captured their transformations, and they left behind clues. Along Marguerite Bay on the western Antarctic Peninsula, ridges of rocks and debris mark former glacier margins. For decades, scientists lacked direct evidence about when many of these ridges formed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Computational model extends the study of nanostructures beyond classic layered systems
item.description: Since the production of graphene in 2004, two-dimensional materials have been sparking scientific and technological interest. As they are only a few atomic layers thick, or even just a single atomic layer, they can exhibit special electronic, magnetic or chemical properties—which make them particularly interesting for applications such as electronics, catalysis and energy storage. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rice plants can fight off devastating disease after gene editing with AI-designed tool
item.description: University of Missouri researchers have created rice plants that resist bacterial blight, a devastating disease that threatens one of the world's most important food crops. The advance could help farmers in parts of Asia and Africa, where the disease can destroy harvests and threaten livelihoods. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient Ecuadorian genomes reveal 1,500 years of genetic continuity along Pacific coast
item.description: Ancient genomes from coastal Ecuador reveal 1,500 years of genetic continuity in an understudied part of the ancient world. John Lindo and colleagues sequenced four genomes from individuals excavated at Salango on Ecuador's central coast, dating to around 2,300 years ago, 1,900 years ago and 740 years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What makes us human? Researchers compare brain development in humans and great apes
item.description: How did the human brain become so much larger than that of our closest evolutionary relatives? Part of the answer lies not in new genes, but in how humans and non-human apes use the genes they share. Using brain organoids grown from stem cells, an international team led by Prof. Mareike Albert at TUD Dresden University of Technology compared early brain development in humans, chimpanzees, and gorillas. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Autonomous rendezvous system overcomes simulated spacecraft failures in lab tests
item.description: There is a problem in low Earth orbit, and it's growing. According to the European Space Agency, there are about 19,440 satellites on orbit, 3,540 of which are nonfunctioning and/or not emitting a signal to warn other spacecraft of their location. The need to service these sleepwalking satellites in space will only increase as more are launched. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cooperation in fish: Study reveals a social complexity seen mainly in birds, mammals
item.description: In some group-living animals, individuals other than the parents help care for offspring. This breeding system, known as cooperative breeding, is thought to have evolved from monogamous family groups in which offspring remain in their natal group and engage in various cooperative behaviors, including helping to care for younger siblings. Cooperative breeding has been documented in mammals and birds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dino skeleton that looks like mini T. rex sells for a giant US$47 million
item.description: A dinosaur that looks like a miniature T. rex is now one of the world’s most expensive fossils. The rare skeleton of a Nanotyrannus – recently confirmed to be a distant cousin of Tyrannosaurus rex, not just a young specimen – sold for US$47.3 million to a mystery buyer at auction in New York on Tuesday, according to Sotheby’s. The auction house had expected it to fetch anywhere from US$6 to US$9 million. The blockbuster price tag for “Jodi”, as the skeleton is nicknamed, makes it the... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Reusable palladium catalyst enables more direct chemical synthesis
item.description: Making complex molecules often means joining smaller chemical building blocks together, a process facilitated by catalysts, compounds that make such reactions possible or speed them up without being consumed themselves. Many widely used reactions also require chemists to modify their starting molecules before joining them. These added chemical "handles" make the molecules reactive, but preparing them means extra steps and, often, additional waste. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How native stingless bees are helping to combat antimicrobial resistance
item.description: New research from the University of Sydney expands the potential medicinal benefits of honey and propolis (the plant resin and beeswax mixture bees use to build their nests) produced by Australia's stingless bees. Building on earlier research, a study led by Ph.D. candidate Jasmin Li tested the honey and propolis against bacterial and fungal pathogens. The honey was active against all bacteria tested, including species that are a growing concern for antimicrobial resistance, such as hard-to-treat hospital bacteria Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Botanists comb Gabon's rich rainforests with nature on the line
item.description: Each year, Gabon's lush rainforests yield the discovery of previously unknown plant species to botanists like Archange Boupoya, who believes that this exceptional yet largely mysterious natural wealth needs cataloguing to save. Fuente: Africanews.

item.title: NASA Invites Media to Crew Completion of Yearlong Mars Simulation
item.description: The four volunteers who lived and worked in a simulated NASA Mars mission for more than a year will exit their habitat on Saturday, Oct. 31, after 378 days of isolation in a facility at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. Health and performance data collected from the simulation can help NASA develop methods […] Fuente: NASA.
